query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based models and simulations describe triboelectric charging of powders during feeding, conveying and dosing (condenser model, work-function or surface-state models, DEM with charge transfer plus Coulomb and image forces, CFD-DEM with electrostatics), particularly contacts between metal or salt particles and polymer walls (PLA, PETG, nylon); the effect of humidity and of inert gases (argon, nitrogen) on charge relaxation and gas breakdown; and adhesion of charged fine particles to walls? Which open-source codes implement this, which parameters are needed, and how were the simulations validated (Faraday-cup charge-to-mass ratio)?
task_summary: Physics Models Codes Parameters And Validation For Triboelectric Charging During Powder Feeding And Dosing

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: update_plan

Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.

    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,

- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):

Supported Enums:

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

Abstract:
Atmospheric transport and suspension of dust frequently brings electrification, which may be substantial. Electric fields of 10 kV m−1 to 100 kV m−1 have been observed at the surface beneath suspended dust in the terrestrial atmosphere, and some electrification has been observed to persist in dust at levels to 5 km, as well as in volcanic plumes. The interaction between individual particles which causes the electrification is incompletely understood, and multiple processes are thought to be acting. A variation in particle charge with particle size, and the effect of gravitational separation explains to, some extent, the charge structures observed in terrestrial dust storms. More extensive flow-based modelling demonstrates that bulk electric fields in excess of 10 kV m−1 can be obtained rapidly (in less than 10 s) from rotating dust systems (dust devils) and that terrestrial breakdown fields can be obtained. Modelled profiles of electrical conductivity in the Martian atmosphere suggest the possibility of dust electrification, and dust devils have been suggested as a mechanism of charge separation able to maintain current flow between one region of the atmosphere and another, through a global circuit. Fundamental new understanding of Martian atmospheric electricity will result from the ExoMars mission, which carries the DREAMS (Dust characterization, Risk Assessment, and Environment Analyser on the Martian Surface)—MicroARES (Atmospheric Radiation and Electricity Sensor) instrumentation to Mars in 2016 for the first in situ electrical measurements.

Abstract:
Abstract:   Multiferroics are a novel class of next generation multifunctional materials that exhibit simultaneous magnetic spin, electric dipole, and ferroelastic ordering. It gives an additional degree of freedom to design new devices. Magnetoelectric effect in these materials result in the manipulation of magnetic spins via applied electric field and vice versa, making them suitable for next generation applications. Single phase multiferroics show low magnetoelectric coefficient, hence there is a need to look at composite multiferroic structures with respective magnetic and ferroelectric phase. The magnetoelectric coefficient in the composite structures depends on the magnitude of strain induced by one phase to the other. This requires the need to study suitable magnetic and ferroelectric materials that can be combined to create magnetoelectric multiferroic composite structures. Also, higher surface to volume ratio at the nanoscale should enhance the interaction between the two phases. Here, in we synthesised and studied magnetic and ferroelectric structures that have potential to be used as the respective phases of multiferroic magnetoelectric composites.  Magnetic materials with high magnetostriction and low coercivity are suitable candidates for the formation of multiferroic composite. The size dependent and tuneable magnetic properties of cobalt ferrite and nickel-iron composites, respectively fulfil the above-mentioned criteria. Herein, the properties of the above magnetic materials were explored at nanoscale where efficient techniques such as thermal decomposition and electrospinning were applied. Cobalt ferrite nanoparticles with varying sizes were synthesised at the nanoscale and magnetic studies were performed to study their size dependent suitability to be used as a potential magnetic material in multiferroic composite formation. The nanoparticle synthesis by thermal decomposition of metal oleate precursors displayed reaction time dependent growth. The nanoparticles sized below superparamagnetic limit showed a negligible coercivity fulfilling an essential requirement to display magnetoelectric effect. Alongside, a successful synthesis of novel cobalt iron oxide (Co0.33Fe0.67O) nanoparticles was also performed. This displayed a synthesis dependent ferrimagnetic to antiferromagnetic phase transition in Co Fe-O structure at nanoscale. A controlled oxidation of Co0.33Fe0.67O could lead to the formation of antiferromagnetic-ferrimagnetic core-shell nanostructure that can overcome the superparamagnetic limit in nanoparticles system. They are potential materials in ME-RAMs. 1-D magnetic nanostructure show a sharp shape anisotropy and hence can be used as magnetic components of composite multiferroic structures. Nickel-iron composites in FCC phase were studied at the nanoscale in the form of fibres. Electrospinning of suitable metal precursors with PVP polymer followed by the reduction of nanofibres in H2 led to the formation of Ni0.47Fe0.53 fibre mats. They were ferromagnetic and displayed high saturation magnetisation along with low coercivity fulfilling the requirement to be used in magnetoelectric applications.   1-D flexible ferroelectric composite structures were studied alongside to be used as the ferroelectric component of multiferroic composites. Polyvinylidene fluoride was doped with DIPAB at varying ratios to study the improvement in the ferroelectric properties of the composite structure in comparison to just PVDF with low dielectric constant. Electrospinning of composite polymer solution led to the formation of DIPAB doped PVDF nanofibres. They displayed improved relative dielectric constant and low loss tangent and find use in composite magnetoelectric materials formation. The ease of processability of DIPAB doped PVDF nanofibres aids in incorporating the above studied magnetic materials.  The studies proved the worth of as-synthesised magnetic and ferroelectric materials at the nanoscale for the formation of magnetoelectric multiferroic composite nanomaterials. The cobalt ferrite nanoparticles doped in DIPAB-PVDF nanofibres can result in core-sheath ME composite structure. A coating of DIPAB-PVDF composite on the formed Ni0.47Fe0.53 fibres will result to the formation of 1-D magnetoelectric structures.

Abstract:
Three-dimensional (3D) printing, alternatively known as additive manufacturing, is a transformative technology enabling precise, customized, and efficient manufacturing of components with complex structures. It revolutionizes traditional processes, allowing rapid prototyping, cost-effective production, and intricate designs. The 3D printed graphene-based materials combine graphene’s exceptional properties with additive manufacturing’s versatility, offering precise control over intricate structures with enhanced functionalities. To gain comprehensive insights into the development of 3D printed graphene and graphene/polymer composites, this review delves into their intricate fabrication methods, unique structural attributes, and multifaceted applications across various domains. Recent advances in printable materials, apparatus characteristics, and printed structures of typical 3D printing techniques for graphene and graphene/polymer composites are addressed, including extrusion methods (direct ink writing and fused deposition modeling), photopolymerization strategies (stereolithography and digital light processing) and powder-based techniques. Multifunctional applications in energy storage, physical sensor, stretchable conductor, electromagnetic interference shielding and wave absorption, as well as bio-applications are highlighted. Despite significant advancements in 3D printed graphene and its polymer composites, innovative studies are still necessary to fully unlock their inherent capabilities.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Polymer powder bed fusion (PBF) is strongly influenced by powder chemistry and powder state, yet many studies discuss the materials and processing conditions in isolation. This review synthesises the literature using a powder-centred framework that connects polymer chemistry and powder production history to measurable powder descriptors, and then links these descriptors to processing windows, defect mechanisms, and application outcomes. Key descriptors include crystallinity and thermal transitions, additive packages, particle size distribution, morphology, and surface texture. Environmental sensitivities are also considered, including moisture uptake, temperature effects, and optical response. These factors are related to powder spreading, energy absorption, and melt solidification or sintering to explain how flowability, packing density, and melt dynamics govern porosity, lack of fusion, distortion, and degradation. Powder qualification is discussed together with lot-to-lot variability and lifecycle effects, including ageing, reuse, and refresh, using the indicators commonly reported in laboratory and production settings and supported by emerging in situ monitoring. Application case studies are consolidated to illustrate how powder state and process control translate into repeatable qualification targets as polymer PBF moves toward a predictable and transferable manufacturing practice.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000000

From text 'pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 31-35'.

C Pei. Dem-cfd analysis of contact electrification and electrostatic interactions during powder handling processes. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt provides quantitative physics-based models for metal–metal and polymer–metal triboelectric charging. For separated metal surfaces treated as a capacitor, the equilibrium transferred charge is Δq_e = C_0V_c, where C_0 is the effective capacitance and V_c is the contact potential difference (CPD); the charge on the two materials is equal and opposite. For polymer particles contacting conductive metals, the single-contact model is Δq = k_sS(V_s − V_p − V′) = k_sS(V_s − V_p − k_0q), where k_s is a charging constant, S is maximum contact area, V_s and V_p are effective work-function potentials, and the induced potential is proportional to particle charge. Under uniform charge distribution, k_0 is related to separation distance and particle radius through k_0 = z/(4πε_0r_p²) as presented in the excerpt. Repeated contacts produce charge accumulation until induced potential equals CPD, giving q∞ = (V_s − V_p)/k_0; the approach to equilibrium is exponential with contact number, analogous to first-order kinetics. Experiments cited include Lowell, Matsusaka et al., Watanabe et al., Kittaka, Davies, Matsuyama and Yamamoto, and others. The excerpt notes Faraday-cage charge measurements and Kelvin work-function measurements, while charge dissipation is described as exponential. It does not provide DEM-CFD Poisson/image-force equations, humidity results, wall adhesion data, or a complete validation study.

From text 'pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 77-82'.

C Pei. Dem-cfd analysis of contact electrification and electrostatic interactions during powder handling processes. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt is relevant to DEM-CFD modelling of triboelectric charging and electrostatic interactions, but it does not provide the requested detailed condenser-capacitor, effective-work-function, insulator-surface-state, contact-area, leakage, humidity, Faraday-cup, or polymer-wall-adhesion formulations. It identifies several useful modelling approaches and validation studies. Pei et al. (2010) coupled DEM-CFD with electrostatic interactions using a direct-truncation (DT) method and simulated deposition of bi-charged microparticles; electrostatic forces produced agglomerate formation and breakage. Hassani et al. (2013) used DEM-CFD for charged particles in gas-solid fluidized beds, with Coulomb forces and a DT cutoff defined where electrostatic force fell below 5% of particle weight. Their simulations found smaller bubbles and more homogeneous beds for mono-charged particles, and particle chains for bi-charged particles. Liu et al. (2010) combined DEM, a boundary-element method for near-surface fields, and adaptive multipole expansion for distant charges, predicting chain-like aggregates on electrodes. Hogue et al. (2008) used the exponential charging model q(t)=qa(1−exp(−kct)), with unscreened or screened Coulomb forces. Šupuk et al. (2011) experimentally and numerically studied lactose, hydroxypropyl cellulose, and alumina charging in shaking capsules of several wall materials; including long-range Coulomb forces improved agreement with measured charging accumulation. The excerpt also cautions that the time-dependent model is unsuitable for complicated dynamics or enduring random contacts.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 35-40'.

C Pei. Dem-cfd analysis of contact electrification and electrostatic interactions during powder handling processes. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt reviews quantitative physics-based models for contact and frictional electrification. The condenser model treats transferred charge as proportional to existing particle charge, analogous to first-order kinetics, producing exponential charge accumulation with contact number. Matsusaka et al. (2000) validated this exponential behavior for a rubber sphere repeatedly impacting a metal plate, including exponential charge dissipation. Matsuyama and Yamamoto (1995a) introduced an image-effect correction for polarization of the metal plate and a charge-relaxation model in which tunneling transfers charge during contact, while gaseous discharge during separation reduces charge once the potential difference exceeds a critical value. The excerpt notes that assuming a 1 nm separation overpredicts equilibrium charge because surface topology creates a larger effective gap. For insulator-insulator contacts, Castle and Schein’s (1995) surface-state model relates charge per contact area to effective work-function differences and the induced electric field, resembling the condenser model. McCarty and Whitesides (2008) caution that electron transfer requires suitably matched donor and acceptor orbitals. Alternative ion-transfer and material-transfer mechanisms depend on surface structure and material properties; experiments by Diaz and colleagues and McCarty et al. observed mobile-ion transfer and air-discharge-limited charge proportional to surface area. Friction experiments also show greater charge transfer with changing contact area.

## pqac-00000005

From text 'pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 102-107'.

C Pei. Dem-cfd analysis of contact electrification and electrostatic interactions during powder handling processes. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt describes C. Pei’s 2014 DEM-CFD study of contact electrification for spherical particles, using a condenser model coupled to particle dynamics and fluidization. The model predicts that charge accumulation over repeated impacts follows an exponential approach to saturation. Equilibrium charge depends on particle diameter and contact potential difference (CPD), with equilibrium charge proportional to diameter squared and therefore to particle surface area under a uniform surface-charge assumption. Smaller particles have lower total equilibrium charge but higher charge-to-mass ratios, making electrostatic forces more important relative to gravity. The transferred charge during impact with a conductive substrate is proportional to maximum contact area; Hertz theory relates contact area to impact velocity and particle radius, while the resulting charging rate is predicted to depend primarily on impact velocity. In fluidized beds, grounded conductive walls generate initial charging, after which particle-particle transfer and mixing redistribute charge until saturation. Increasing excess/superficial gas velocity increases the charging coefficient and accelerates saturation; reported charging coefficients are 1.34, 2.32, and 2.60 s^-1 for excess velocities of 80, 180, and 230 mm s^-1. The model was validated against published experiments, but neglecting charge relaxation and dissipation can overestimate charge for longer impact intervals. The excerpt does not provide effective-work-function, surface-state, humidity, polymer-adhesion, Faraday-cup, Poisson/image-force, or detailed leakage formulations.

## pqac-00000006

From text 'walton2007adhesionoflunar pages 14-16'.

OR Walton. Adhesion of lunar dust. Unknown journal, 2007.

The excerpt identifies Walton as the report author and cites Sternovsky et al. (2002) as the principal experimental work. Their apparatus repeatedly contacted and separated fine particles from metal surfaces, then captured tribocharged particles in a Faraday cup to determine typical charge per particle. For JSC-1 lunar simulant, charging varied with metal work function; oxidized Zr, V, stainless steel, and W behaved similarly, while oxidation-resistant metals showed charging that increased as work function decreased. The reported interpretation is that charging rate is proportional to work-function difference, giving an estimated JSC-1 particle work function of approximately 5.9 eV, slightly lower for smaller particles. The excerpt explicitly cautions that this value is for simulant, not actual lunar regolith, and calls for uncontaminated lunar samples. It does not provide condenser-capacitor, insulator-surface-state, contact-area, charge-saturation, leakage, humidity, polymer-wall, DEM/CFD, or Poisson-equation models. It does provide a quantitative conductive-surface image-charge model: a point-charge force based on an opposite image charge, and an approximate finite dielectric-particle expression, FI ≈ −αQ²/(16πε₀R²), with α = 1.9 for dielectric constant κ = 4. As a validation example, xerographic toner measurements exceeded the uniform-surface-charge image-force prediction by factors of 5–50; a 10 μm toner particle with 15 mC/kg charge-to-mass ratio had Q ≈ 8 fC and calculated image force about 10 nN.

From text 'pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 87-92'.

C Pei. Dem-cfd analysis of contact electrification and electrostatic interactions during powder handling processes. Unknown journal, 2014.

The excerpt describes C. Pei’s 2014 DEM-CFD contact-electrification model for spherical particles. It uses a condenser/contact-potential framework in which the charge transferred during collision m is Δq_m = k_s S_m ΔV_m, with S the maximum contact area, ΔV the total potential difference, and k_s approximately 10^-4 C·m^-2·V^-1. The charging process is expressed as dq/dn = k_s SΔV, where n is collision number. Particle and wall material work functions are assigned, and the maximum contact area is recorded throughout each collision. For an insulating sphere impacting grounded steel, the model uses dq/dn = k_s S(V_s − V_p − k_0q), with V_s = 4.70 V, V_p = 4.52 V, k_s = 1×10^-4 C·m^-2·V^-1, separation distance z = 260 nm, and k_0 = 1.0×10^7 V·C^-1. The resulting charge approaches q∞ = (V_s−V_p)/k_0 exponentially with collision number, with charging coefficient k_c = k_sSk_0. Validation against Matsusaka et al. (2000) used successive impacts at 0.5–4.0 m·s^-1, initial charges −5, 0, and 5 nC, and particle diameters of 5–31 mm; simulations agreed closely with measured transferred charge and charge accumulation. This excerpt does not cover Poisson/image forces, Faraday-cup measurements, humidity, polymer-wall adhesion, or explicit surface-state/leakage models; relaxation and dissipation were neglected.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Magnetic granular matter extends classical granular physics through the introduction of tunable, long-range dipolar interactions. These interactions give rise to a wide range of collective phenomena, including field-aligned chain formation, enhanced cohesion, anisotropic stress transmission, field and modified flow behaviour. This review summarizes recent experimental, numerical, and theoretical developments in magnetic granular systems, with particular emphasis on the distinction between quasi-static and dynamically driven systems. Existing modelling approaches are discussed, including discrete particle simulations, continuum descriptions, and reduced-order frameworks for capturing the interplay between magnetic interactions and granular dynamics. As an illustrative example, we discuss a minimal lattice-based model motivated by experimentally observed field-induced structural transitions in magnetic granular mounds. The model provides a conceptual framework for exploring how long-range interactions can modify threshold dynamics and instability mechanisms in cohesive granular systems. Finally, we highlight open questions concerning instability thresholds, rheology, avalanche dynamics, multiphysics coupling, and the development of predictive models, and identify promising directions for future experimental and theoretical research.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Binder jetting (BJT) has been extensively explored for additive manufacturing of ceramics due to its ability to create complex structures by processing refractory and hard-to-machine materials. However, achieving a uniform powder bed with high packing density while processing ceramics in BJT remains a challenge. This study systematically examines the role of powder size, powder temperature, flow behavior, and powder size distribution on powder bed formation and resulting part properties. Four different alumina powder sizes (1 μm, 5 μm, 10 μm, and 20 μm) were investigated. Flowability characterizations reveal that 1 μm powder remains poorly flowable at both room and elevated temperatures, while 20 μm powder demonstrates excellent flowability at both temperatures. Smaller powders, especially 1 μm, exhibit around 25% loss in moisture, which results in pronounced agglomeration at room temperature. Discrete element method simulations were used to identify the ideal mixing ratio of the bimodal powder using 5 μm and 20 μm powders. For bimodal powder, both the simulation and the experiments exhibited a preferential deposition of smaller powders in the spreading direction. However, the 5 μm and 20 μm powders did not show any preferential deposition in the simulation, but experiments showed preferential deposition behavior. When using bimodal powder, packing density decreases by 7.65% along the spreading direction, which aligns with an 8.19% drop in part relative density. These findings offer valuable insights into the effects of bimodal powder distribution for controlling powder bed packing density and potentially leveraging spatial density variations for functional applications such as biomedical implants, heat exchangers, and gas filtration.

This excerpt documents a charged-particle extension to LIGGGHTS-PUBLIC, explicitly identified as GNU GPL v2.0 software. The implementation modifies contact handling by adding a global per-particle contact counter, because the native pairwise collision counter resets after a contact breaks. Electrical conduction is modeled using particle work functions and conductivities, Hertzian contact area, an effective conductivity, electric fields at the contact, and Ohm’s law to compute charge transfer over each timestep. Transfer is clipped at the theoretical amount needed to reach equal electric potentials while conserving total charge. Initial validation used two charged spherical particles with varied radii, initial charges, and conductivity; simulations ran after first contact until equipotential conditions were reached. Reported trends include neutralization for equal-magnitude opposite charges, equal nonzero equilibrium charges for equal radii with unequal initial magnitudes, differing final charges for unequal radii, and increasing equilibration time with particle size. A triboelectric charging function was also introduced using work-function differences and contact area, with homogeneous charge distribution assumed at each timestep. Limitations include unresolved multiple-count events within a single elastic contact, reliance on spherical/center-of-mass charge assumptions, and the need for non-spherical geometries and nonuniform dielectric charge distributions. Abstract:
Triboelectrostatic separation is a promising method used to separate non-conductive minerals. However, the knowledge about the underlying triboelectrification mechanisms is still very limited. Thus, predicting the separation results and finding proper separation parameters are challenging tasks.This article presents a comprehensive summary of phenomena and factors which play a decisive role in the charging behavior of non-conductors and, by implication, the efficiency of the separation process, such as water and adsorbents layers on the surface, surface roughness, humidity, type of contact, etc. The authors hope that this article opens a way for a systematic approach through basic experiments dedicated to a better understanding of triboelectrification processes.ZusammenfassungDie Elektroscheidung nach Triboaufladung stellt eine vielversprechende Methode zur Trennung nicht leitfähiger Mineralphasen dar. Das begrenzte Wissen über die zugrundeliegenden Mechanismen der Triboaufladung macht die Vorhersage von über einzustellende Prozessparameter zu erzielenden Trennergebnissen zu einer herausfordernden Aufgabe.Diese Veröffentlichung gibt einen umfassenden Überblick über Phänomene und Faktoren, die eine entscheidende Rolle beim Aufladeverhalten von Nichtleitern spielen oder spielen können und die damit Einfluss auf die Effizienz der Trennung nehmen. Solche Faktoren können sein: Wasser- und Adsorbatschichten, Oberflächenrauigkeit, Luftfeuchtigkeit, Kontaktart, usw. Die Autoren hoffen, dass dieser Artikel Wege für einen systematischen Ansatz durch grundlegende Experimente aufzeigt und damit zu einem besseren Verständnis der bei der Triboaufladung wirkenden Faktoren beiträgt.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Electrical charges play a key role in particle-particle interactions during transport and deposition of volcanic ash with significant impact on their atmospheric residence time, as they can influence aggregation processes. Nonetheless, direct field measurements are rare due to logistic challenges, resulting in a very limited understanding of charge generation and aggregation mechanisms. This study introduces VoltAsh, a cost-effective, portable device for measuring the charge and velocity of settling volcanic ash particles using a Through-Type Faraday Cage (TTFC) and a charge amplifier circuit. Laboratory validation confirmed the accuracy of both charge and velocity measurements when compared with state-of-the-art techniques. Field deployments at Sakurajima volcano (Japan) in November 2023 enabled automated, semi-continuous measurements over several hours, detecting particle charges ranging from 0.5 to 250 pC and velocities up to 5 ms

Abstract:
<jats:p>The demand for flexible and wearable electronics has intensified the need for conformable, high-performance, and self-sustaining power sources. Flexible supercapacitors (FSCs) and flexible batteries (e.g., lithium-ion and lithium–sulfur) are promising owing to their high-power density, long cycle life, and mechanical flexibility. A transformative solution lies in integrating these storage devices with mechanical energy harvesters, particularly triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs), to create autonomous self-charging power systems (SCPSs). TENGs exhibit high output, versatile operational modes, material flexibility, and efficient energy harvesting from body movements. This review provides an overview of the recent advances in flexible energy storage technologies, encompassing carbon-based materials, MXenes, polymers, metal oxides, metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), and their hybrid architectures. It discusses the synergistic integration of these storage devices with TENGs to realize multifunctional SCPSs. It also highlights the fundamental design principles of flexible devices, the critical interplay of materials and architecture, and the journey towards monolithic system integration. The review also underscores the importance of managing harvesters’ pulsed output for efficient storage. Finally, a critical analysis of the challenges, including the energy density–flexibility compromise, environmental stability, and safety, is presented, alongside a forward-looking perspective on commercialization pathways for these technologies to power the next generation of autonomous wearable and sustainable electronic systems.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Polyimine-based composites have emerged as a promising class of dynamic covalent thermosets, combining high mechanical strength, thermal stability, self-healing, recyclability, and reprocessability. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in polyimine synthesis, highlighting dynamic covalent chemistry (DCC) strategies such as imine exchange and reversible Schiff base reactions. Structural customization can be achieved by incorporating reinforcing phases such as carbon nanotubes, graphene, and bio-based fibers. Advanced fabrication methods—including solution casting, hot pressing, and interfacial polymerization—enable precise integration of these components while preserving structural integrity and adaptability. Mechanical performance analysis emphasizes the interplay between dynamic bonds, interfacial engineering, and multiscale design strategies. Polyimine composites exhibit outstanding performance characteristics, including a self-healing efficiency exceeding 90%, a tensile strength reaching 96.2 MPa, and remarkable chemical recyclability. Emerging engineering applications encompass sustainable green materials, flexible electronics, energy storage devices, and flame-retardant systems. Key challenges include balancing multifunctionality, enhancing large-scale processability, and developing low-energy recycling strategies. ## pqac-00000016

From text 'mirkowska2016principalfactorsof pages 9-11'.

Monika Mirkowska, Markus Kratzer, Christian Teichert, and Helmut Flachberger. Principal factors of contact charging of minerals for a successful triboelectrostatic separation process – a review. BHM Berg- und Hüttenmännische Monatshefte, 161:359-382, Aug 2016. URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00501-016-0515-1, doi:10.1007/s00501-016-0515-1. This article has 63 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt supports a non-universal, thickness-dependent role for humidity and surface water in triboelectric charging of insulating minerals and, by implication, other powders or polymers. Ambient surfaces generally carry adsorbed water containing mobile ions. A thin water layer or water bridge can enhance ion-mediated charging: contact permits mobile ions to diffuse between surfaces, while separation kinetically traps some ions on the opposing surface, producing charge. In contrast, a thick or bulk aqueous layer increases surface conductivity and promotes charge leakage or discharging through the mobile-ion-containing Gouy–Chapman layer. The excerpt also notes that hydroxide and hydron separation may contribute, and that acidic or basic surface groups can promote water adsorption and supply H+ and OH− ions. These mechanisms do not establish a universal humidity trend; the outcome depends on water-layer thickness, surface chemistry, ion mobility, and hydrophilicity. The provided pages contain no concrete comparison of argon versus nitrogen carrier gas, no measurements of gas-dependent charge changes, and no discussion of electrical breakdown or Paschen behavior. Thus, they cannot support claims about inert-gas identity or breakdown thresholds.

## pqac-00000017

From text 'peltonen2019electrostaticinstrumentationand pages 35-38'.

J Peltonen. Electrostatic instrumentation and measurements on powders and powder mixtures. Unknown journal, 2019.

The excerpt provides limited but relevant evidence that humidity and temperature can reduce powder charging through changes in electrical resistivity. It reports that increased temperature decreased charging values because resistivity fell, and that sugar powder’s volume resistivity decreased exponentially as humidity or temperature increased. For uncoated insulators, one cited interpretation is that surface-resistivity measurements primarily reflect adsorbed surface water; under a strong electric field, water molecules may form conductive chains. These observations support a leakage-based mechanism in which adsorbed moisture increases conductivity and accelerates charge dissipation, rather than establishing a universal humidity effect on triboelectric charging. The excerpt does not provide concrete experiments on polymer surface ions, capillary cohesion, or a systematic separation of moisture-mediated charge transfer from post-charging leakage. It also contains no information about argon versus nitrogen carrier gases, gas-dependent charging, electrical breakdown, or Paschen-law behavior. The Faraday-cup and induction-probe descriptions concern charge measurement methods, not those gas-comparison models. Thus, this passage supports only cautious claims about humidity-associated resistivity and charge decay.

## pqac-00000018

From text 'heinert2021hiddeninvolvementof pages 77-81'.

C Heinert. Hidden involvement of liquids and gases in electrostatic charging. Unknown journal, 2021.

The excerpt is a bibliography rather than a results section, so it does not provide concrete measurements or model outputs establishing how humidity controls powder/polymer triboelectric charging. It identifies relevant work on atmospheric water and surface charge: water-vapor adsorption on silica, atmospheric-water effects on polyethylene charge buildup and dissipation, and surface-charge decay on polymeric materials under different neutralization modes in air. These references suggest that humidity/water adsorption and leakage or neutralization are studied variables, but the excerpt does not state whether humidity increases or decreases charge, nor does it quantify capillary cohesion or distinguish universal from material-specific behavior. It also cites work on electrostatic charge generation and wall fouling in gas–solid fluidized beds, but gives no comparison of carrier gases. No cited title or passage here reports argon-versus-nitrogen experiments, gas-specific charge magnitudes, electrical-breakdown thresholds, or Paschen-law behavior. The bibliography does include references on charge decay in air and sulfur hexafluoride and on atmospheric ions, clouds, aerosols, and atmospheric electricity, but these cannot support specific conclusions about argon, nitrogen, or breakdown without the underlying papers. Therefore, the excerpt mainly points to relevant literature and emphasizes that water-related charging and leakage require measurement-specific interpretation.

Abstract:
The effects of water and temperature on the triboelectrification of granular materials have been reported by numerous authors, but have not been studied robustly in the context of volcanic plumes. Here, we present the results of a set of experiments designed to elucidate how environmental conditions modulate the triboelectric characteristics of volcanic ash in the upper region of the convective column. We find that small amounts of water can reduce the charge collected by submillimeter‐sized ash grains by up to an order of magnitude. Increasing temperature at a constant relative humidity also appears to decrease the amount of charge gained by particles. Analysis of our data shows that if particles undergo low‐energy, low‐frequency collisions in humid environments under minute‐long time scales, charge dissipation dominates over charge accumulation. Thus, our work suggests that triboelectric charging may be an inefficient electrification mechanism outside of the gas‐thrust region where collision energies and rates are high and residence times are low.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Hydrogen and some of its derivatives (such as e-methanol, e-methane, and e-ammonia) are promising energy carriers that have the potential to replace conventional fuels, thereby eliminating their harmful environmental impacts. An innovative use of hydrogen as a zero-emission fuel is being a source of weakly-ionized plasma through seeding its combustion products with a small amount of an alkali metal vapor (cesium or potassium). This plasma can be used as the working fluid in supersonic open-cycle magnetohydrodynamic (OCMHD) power generators. In such OCMHD generators, direct-current (DC) electricity is generated directly without moving turbogenerators. In the current study, we quantitatively and qualitatively explore the levels of electric conductivity and the resultant volumetric electric output power density in a typical OCMHD supersonic channel, where thermal equilibrium plasma is accelerated at a Mach number of two (Mach 2) while being subject to a strong applied magnetic field (applied magnetic-field flux density) of five teslas (5 T), and with the assumption of an isothermal temperature of 2,300 K (2,026.85 &deg;C). We varied the total pressure of the pre-ionization seeded gas mixture between 1/16 atm and 16 atm. We varied the seed level between 0.0625% and 16% (pre-ionization mole fraction). We varied the seed type between cesium and potassium. We varied the oxidizer type between air (oxygen-nitrogen mixture, 21%-79% by mole) and pure oxygen. Our results suggest that the ideal power density can reach exceptional levels beyond 1,000 MW/m3 (or 1 kW/cm3). The power density can be enhanced using any of the following techniques: (1) lower total pressures, (2) using cesium instead of potassium for seeding, and (3) using air instead of oxygen as an oxidizer (if the temperature is unchanged). A seed level between 1% and 4% (pre-ionization mole fraction) is recommended (much lower or much higher seed levels are harmful to the OCMHD performance). The seed level that maximizes the electric power is not necessarily the same seed level that maximizes the electric conductivity due to additional thermochemical changes caused by the additive seed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The effects of various fundamental forces on the adhesion of fine dust particles are reviewed. The particle-size and distance variation of surface-energy related (e.g., van der Waals) forces are compared to similar relations for static-electric image-forces for tribo-charged particles near (or contacting) conducting surfaces. The van der Waals force (between macroscopic spheres), a patchcharge image-force and static-electric image-forces all exhibit an inverse square variation with distance; however, these forces have dramatically different ranges-of-effect. The very short-range nature of van der Waals forces (of order 10nm) is a major reason that most real contacts, involving non-smooth surfaces, exhibit adhesion forces that are substantially lower than values predicted for smooth particles. Based on studies of Lunar and Martian regolith stimulant powders, triboelectric charges on fine particles appear to scale linearly with particle size. It is shown that below some threshold size, the adhesion (to conducting surfaces) of charged dust particles possessing such a linear charge-to-size scaling relationship, may be dominated by image-charge forces, instead of surface-energy related interactions. This is counter to what might have been expected from a cursory examination of the fundamental force relations, which would suggest van der Waals adhesion forces would dominate for small particle sizes.

Abstract:
The 2022 Roadmap is the next update in the series of Plasma Roadmaps published by Journal of Physics D with the intent to identify important outstanding challenges in the field of low-temperature plasma (LTP) physics and technology. The format of the Roadmap is the same as the previous Roadmaps representing the visions of 41 leading experts representing 21 countries and five continents in the various sub-fields of LTP science and technology. In recognition of the evolution in the field, several new topics have been introduced or given more prominence. These new topics and emphasis highlight increased interests in plasma-enabled additive manufacturing, soft materials, electrification of chemical conversions, plasma propulsion, extreme plasma regimes, plasmas in hypersonics, data-driven plasma science and technology and the contribution of LTP to combat COVID-19. In the last few decades, LTP science and technology has made a tremendously positive impact on our society. It is our hope that this roadmap will help continue this excellent track record over the next 5–10 years.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000019

From text 'alois2019contactelectrificationin pages 134-137'.

Stefano Alois. Contact electrification in aerosolized micron-sized solid particles: dependence upon size, chemical composition and gas properties. ArXiv, Jan 2019. URL: https://doi.org/10.14279/depositonce-7810, doi:10.14279/depositonce-7810. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt reports aerosol powder tribocharging experiments using air, argon, and CO2, but it does not report a nitrogen comparison. Charge was measured with a Faraday-tube/injector arrangement, including the total charge of the particle cloud and surface charge concentration. Gas composition affected charging: the mean surface charge did not scale linearly with the gases’ typical breakdown voltages, while charge increased by approximately 50% from argon to CO2. This indicates that gas breakdown voltage alone was not the limiting control on charging and should not be used to infer that an inert gas is antistatic. Most measurements were performed under dry conditions (RH < 2%). For silica, humidity had a major effect, with surface charge concentration increasing by almost tenfold around 50% relative humidity. Gas breakdown was directly observed through rapid, intense injector-tube voltage spikes and glow discharge recorded by a high-speed camera; an individual discharge could lower total generated charge by up to 6%. The excerpt does not provide Paschen-law calculations or explicit atmospheric-pressure versus micron-gap breakdown models. It only notes that contact-site electric fields can greatly exceed dielectric breakdown values over nanometre scales, and that observed discharge may occur between the charged aerosol cloud and injector tube.


---

## pqac-00000020

From text 'springsklee2023experimentalvolcaniclightning pages 63-67'.

Christina Springsklee. Experimental volcanic lightning under early earth conditions: implications for prebiotic synthesis and the origin of life. Dissertation, Jan 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.5282/edoc.32199, doi:10.5282/edoc.32199. This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt gives a direct argon-versus-nitrogen comparison using experiments EXP371 (argon carrier gas) and EXP370 (nitrogen carrier gas), with glass-bead powder decompressed at approximately 10 MPa. Both carrier gases produced aerosol particle charging, observed as an increase in the Faraday-cage net charge. However, visible electrical discharges were less frequent with nitrogen. In the argon experiment, individual discharges reduced the Faraday-cage net charge after the initial charging increase; this discharge-related decrease was not observed in the nitrogen jet. Thus, nitrogen should not be interpreted as intrinsically antistatic: particles still tribocharged, while discharge occurrence or detectability differed. The excerpt also reports that near-vent discharges can occur in oxygen-free atmospheres and that changing the surrounding atmosphere among air, CO2, and CO2-CO did not significantly change discharge magnitude or number under these experimental conditions. It invokes Paschen’s law only generally: breakdown depends on surrounding-gas pressure and electrode/object separation. No dry-versus-humid gas comparison, quantitative humidity result, atmospheric-versus-micron-gap test, or separate Paschen-model calculation is provided here. The cited Paschen discussion should therefore not be extended beyond the stated pressure-and-distance dependence.

Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000021

From text 'carazzetti2009electricalbreakdownat pages 3-4'.

P Carazzetti and H Shea. Electrical breakdown at low pressure for planar microelectromechanical systems with 10-to 500-micron gaps. Unknown journal, 2009.

The excerpt reports actual dc breakdown measurements for He, Ar, and N2, using planar electrode gaps from 10 to 500 micrometers and pressures from 10^2 to 8×10^4 Pa (1–800 mbar). The directly comparable gas data shown are for three devices with a 100-micrometer gap; breakdown voltage was measured five times at each pressure, with averages and minimum/maximum values plotted. Qualitatively, the measured Paschen behavior follows the expected trend: helium has the lowest breakdown voltage, nitrogen the highest, and argon lies between them. The excerpt does not provide a numerical table of argon or nitrogen voltages, does not include air measurements, and does not report electric-field values; fields would require calculating Vbd divided by the gap. It also does not address a 3-mm gap or submicron contacts: the experimental range stops at 500 micrometers, so extrapolation to those geometries is unsupported here. The authors caution that breakdown voltage depends strongly on cathode material and surface roughness, and differs between dc and rf operation. Paschen theory gives the expected overall shape but fits poorly over the full pressure range. No specific discussion of impurities, humidity, or their effects appears in this excerpt.


---

## pqac-00000022

From text 'carazzetti2009electricalbreakdownat pages 8-9'.

P Carazzetti and H Shea. Electrical breakdown at low pressure for planar microelectromechanical systems with 10-to 500-micron gaps. Unknown journal, 2009.

The excerpt reports measurements only for helium, argon, and nitrogen, using planar aluminum electrodes with 10–500 micrometer gaps and pressures from roughly 500 to 8×10^4 Pa (5–800 mbar); it does not provide a direct argon-versus-nitrogen-versus-air numerical comparison, nor measurements at 3 mm or submicron contacts. At sufficiently high pressure or gap (high P·d), classical Paschen scaling is observed for all three tested gases. At low P·d, deviations occur because the mean free path approaches the gap, and because planar structures contain many effective length scales that superpose Paschen curves. The authors state that, at one atmosphere, standard Paschen behavior applies for gaps larger than 10 micrometers, while micron-scale gaps below atmospheric pressure require caution. At low pressure, changing the nominal electrode gap does not necessarily strongly change ignition voltage. The lowest reported helium ignition voltages were 170–210 V for serrated electrodes; helium breakdown is described as significantly lower than nitrogen. Serrated patterns and planar geometry are discussed, but the excerpt does not quantify effects from gas impurities, humidity, electrode surface roughness, or contact-scale field enhancement. Air is mentioned only through cited prior literature, not characterized in the presented measurements.


---

## pqac-00000023

From text 'carazzetti2009electricalbreakdownat pages 5-7'.

P Carazzetti and H Shea. Electrical breakdown at low pressure for planar microelectromechanical systems with 10-to 500-micron gaps. Unknown journal, 2009.

The excerpt reports measured breakdown behavior for helium, argon, and nitrogen in planar MEMS devices with approximately 10–500 µm gaps; it does not provide air data, direct electric-field values, impurity or humidity measurements, or surface-roughness analysis. Argon measurements are shown in Fig. 9 and nitrogen in Fig. 10, with breakdown voltage plotted against pressure and p·d. The data generally collapse under Paschen scaling at sufficiently high reduced pressure, but the Paschen fit is reliable only in the higher-p·d regime. The approximate transition thresholds are p·d ≈ 5 Pa·m for He, 3 Pa·m for Ar, and 2 Pa·m for N₂; below these values, deviations occur, with the transition at lower pressures for He than Ar and N₂. Nitrogen follows standard Paschen scaling for almost all reported measurements. From text 'pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 107-113'.

For triboelectric charging, Pei reports a DEM-CFD condenser model validated against published experimental data. For electrostatics, the chapter introduces long-range interactions in DEM and uses direct pairwise Coulomb-law calculations for particles treated as spherical particles with uniformly distributed, non-polarizable surface charge. Particle-surface interactions with conductive or polarizable surfaces are represented by an image-force expression, also having an inverse-square form. The excerpt therefore supports direct Coulomb and image-force models, not a Poisson-equation field solve. It gives no evidence that Poisson electrostatics, polarization, or image forces are included by default in open-source CFDEM coupling. It also provides no computational-cost comparison between direct summation and Poisson methods. 2.1.3.1  Initial Simulation Results

Initial simulations of two charged particles are conducted to demonstrate the charge
transfer process via triboelectric charging in LIGGGHTS. We vary parameters to
demonstrate the range of conditions that might be explored with the model. The cutoff
distance of charge transfer is set to 250 nm based on the parameter used in Mukherjee
et al. (2016) and Lowell and Rose-Innes (1980). Each pair of particles is given initial
charges of ±10 nC and different combinations of work functions in eight trials as
shown in Table 2. They begin 6 cm away from each other and are attracted toward the
center of the simulation space. When the two particles have the same work function
(3 eV), no charge transfer via tribocharging occurs since the charge transferred depends
on the difference between work functions. As a result, they keep their initial charges.
When the two particles are assigned different work functions, charge transfer occurs.

electrons flow from the particle with the lower work function to the one with the higher
work function since this is the combination with the biggest difference between two
work functions among the four trials for each coefficient of restitution.

Abstract:
Abstract. Machine learning has had an enormous impact in many scientific disciplines. It has also attracted significant interest in the field of low-temperature plasma (LTP) modeling and simulation in past years. Its application should be carefully assessed in general, but many aspects of plasma modeling and simulation have benefited substantially from recent developments within the field of machine learning and data-driven modeling. In this survey, we approach two main objectives: (a) we review the state-of-the-art, focusing on approaches to LTP modeling and simulation. By dividing our survey into plasma physics, plasma chemistry, plasma–surface interactions, and plasma process control, we aim to extensively discuss relevant examples from literature. (b) We provide a perspective of potential advances to plasma science and technology. We specifically elaborate on advances possibly enabled by adaptation from other scientific disciplines. We argue that not only the known unknowns but also unknown unknowns may be discovered due to the inherent propensity of data-driven methods to spotlight hidden patterns in data.

Abstract:
Developing constitutive models for particle phase rheology in gas-fluidized suspensions through rigorous statistical mechanical methods is very difficult when complex inter-particle forces are present. In the present study, we pursue a computational approach based on results obtained through Eulerian–Lagrangian simulations of the fluidized state. Simulations were performed in a periodic domain for non-cohesive and mildly cohesive (Geldart Group A) particles. Based on the simulation results, we propose modified closures for pressure, bulk viscosity, shear viscosity and the rate of dissipation of pseudo-thermal energy. For non-cohesive particles, results in the high granular temperature $T$ regime agree well with constitutive expressions afforded by the kinetic theory of granular materials, demonstrating the validity of the methodology. The simulations reveal a low $T$ regime, where the inter-particle collision time is determined by gravitational fall between collisions. Inter-particle cohesion has little effect in the high $T$ regime, but changes the behaviour appreciably in the low $T$ regime. At a given $T$ , a cohesive particle system manifests a lower pressure at low particle volume fractions when compared to non-cohesive systems; at higher volume fractions, the cohesive assemblies attain higher coordination numbers than the non-cohesive systems, and experience greater pressures. Cohesive systems exhibit yield stress, which is weakened by particle agitation, as characterized by $T$ . All these effects are captured through simple modifications to the kinetic theory of granular materials for non-cohesive materials.

Abstract:
A coupled computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and discrete element method (DEM) model was developed to analyze the fluid-particle and particle-particle interactions in a 3D liquid-solid fluidized bed (LSFB). The CFD-DEM model was validated using the Electrical Resistance Tomography (ERT) experimental method. ERT was employed to measure the bed-averaged particle volume fraction (BPVF) of 0.002 m glass beads fluidized with water for various particle numbers and flow rates. It was found that simulations employing the combination of the Gidaspow drag model with pressure gradient and virtual mass forces provided the least percentage error between experiments and simulations. It was also found that contact parameters must be calibrated to account for the particles being wet. The difference between simulations and experiments was 4.74%. The CFD-DEM model was also employed alongside stability analysis to investigate the hydrodynamic behavior within the LSFB and the intermediate flow regime for all cases studied.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study develops a Bayesian optimization framework to calibrate two discrete element method (DEM) parameters—the cohesion-related surface energy coefficient (k) and the rolling resistance coefficient (μr)—based on experimental void ratio data obtained from powder consolidation tests. The optimized parameter set reproduces the void ratio obtained from the consolidation experiment, demonstrating efficient and physically plausible calibration under confined loading. However, when these parameters are applied to powder spreading simulations, the resulting powder beds become excessively cohesive, leading to poor layer uniformity. This discrepancy is attributed to (i) the mismatch in mechanical scaling (σ/E) between the experimental and simulated conditions and (ii) the shift in dominant particle-scale mechanics from normal-force-controlled consolidation to shear-dominated spreading. The results indicate that DEM parameter calibration for powder bed-based additive manufacturing should incorporate shear-related experimental metrics and scaling considerations rather than rely solely on consolidation-based fitting.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Binder jetting of minimally processed, locally sourced sediments offers a promising route toward sustainable additive manufacturing, but powder spreading of poorly sorted, irregular grains remains underexplored. This study uses high-fidelity Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations to quantify how process parameters govern layer quality when spreading an unrefined sandy silt from the Gypsum Hills, Kansas, USA, with a counter-rotating roller. Twenty-five multi-sphere particle shapes were reconstructed from morphological measurements and used to simulate up to 300,000 interacting grains while systematically varying roller traverse speed, rotational speed, diameter, and layer thickness. Traverse speed and layer thickness emerged as the dominant controls on powder bed density and uniformity: the slowest traverse speed (20 mm/s) produced the highest density (~ 0.50) and lowest variability (~ 0.08), and layer thicknesses ≥ 120 μm were required to avoid jamming and obtain consistent packing. In contrast, roller diameter and rotational speed had only minor influence over the explored ranges. The simulations also revealed percolation-driven segregation, with fine particles preferentially settling beneath coarser grains. Comparison with an idealized spherical powder showed that the silt is intrinsically harder to spread, achieving lower density (0.51 vs. 0.59) and higher variability. These results demonstrate that binder jet processing of unrefined silt is feasible but favors slower spreading and thicker layers that may reduce throughput and resolution, and they provide process design guidelines and particle-scale insight for deploying raw earth feedstocks in sustainable binder jetting.</jats:p>
