contexts.context: For metallic powders used in PBF-LM, DEM parameters were fitted through a sequential Bayesian-optimization procedure. The objective was to minimize the squared error between experimentally measured consolidation powder-bed void ratio and the void ratio predicted by DEM. The resulting parameter set was then used in powder-spreading simulations, providing an independent test rather than fitting directly to spreading behavior. The study also emphasizes enforcing stress–stiffness scaling, such as matching σ/E, during consolidation calibration so that the relevant nondimensional response is preserved. Calibration based only on packing or consolidation density can fail when spreading is shear-dominated because the two tests activate different particle-scale mechanisms. Consolidation is primarily governed by inter-particle normal forces after the particle arrangement becomes partially fixed, whereas spreading involves coater-induced separation, contact-point sliding, tangential forces, irregular particle motion, and localized void formation. Friction and sliding dissipate energy efficiently, so parameter sensitivities and optimal values can differ between the regimes. Consequently, a consolidation-calibrated parameter set may not reproduce spreading accurately. The excerpt identifies direct powder-layer validation observables for a shear-relevant calibration as bulk density, area coverage, and shear metrics; these should be measured during powder-bed formation and compared with DEM predictions.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides quantitative electrostatic adhesion evidence, but it does not directly address PLA, PETG, nylon, conductive-wall comparisons, dielectric-interface image-charge coefficients, JKR/SJKR adhesion, capillary forces, patch-charge sign, induced dipoles, or roughness corrections. Its image-force treatment models a charged spherical particle above a charged powder layer on a conducting substrate, using a simplified point-charge approximation that neglects sphere polarization. It distinguishes repulsive interaction with the charged powder layer from attraction to the substrate image charge, and notes that equal-and-opposite force assumptions require the plate radius to greatly exceed coating thickness. Experiments found corona-charged powder substantially more adhesive than tribocharged powder; adding corona ions to a tribocharged layer produced exceedingly high adhesion. Increasing corona voltage from 50 to 80 kV significantly increased adhesion. In a detachment experiment, 25 µm glass spheres showed forces around 6×10^-9 N, increasing to nearly 1×10^-7 N for 75 µm spheres. A calculated example predicted that particles below 11 µm could be repelled from a 50 µm charged layer, and experiments showed fines present on thin coatings but absent from thicker ones, with progressively coarser deposits. These results are relevant to scaling with particle size and charge-to-mass ratio, but should not be extrapolated directly to dielectric polymer walls without an interface-specific electrostatic model.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative guidance for comparing adhesion mechanisms, but it does not supply the requested dielectric image-charge expression, JKR/SJKR equations, or a quantitative PLA/PETG/nylon-versus-conductor experiment. It states that van der Waals, patch-charge image, and static-electric image forces share an inverse-square distance dependence while having very different effective ranges; van der Waals interactions are extremely short range, approximately 10 nm, so rough, non-smooth contacts can have much lower adhesion than smooth-sphere predictions. Triboelectric charge on fine particles is reported to scale approximately linearly with particle size, and for sufficiently small charged particles adhesion to conducting surfaces may become image-charge dominated rather than van der Waals dominated. Conductive or partially conductive materials can reduce charge buildup and attraction of uncharged particles to charged regions, but grounding does not remove attraction between charged particles and the conductor. For dielectric walls, the excerpt does not establish whether image forces should be treated with an effective permittivity contrast, nor does it discuss whether patch charges are opposite or like, induced dipoles, JKR/SJKR work of adhesion, or material-specific polymer data. Humidity may strongly increase adhesion through capillary bridges when water spans roughness gaps; alternatively it can reduce electrostatic adhesion by charge leakage. Roughness and humidity therefore require explicit control in any quantitative comparison.

contexts.context: The excerpt is directly relevant to electrostatic adhesion of micron powders on conductive walls, but it does not provide the dielectric-interface expression involving (epsilon2−epsilon1)/(epsilon2+epsilon1), nor does it discuss PLA, PETG, nylon, patch-charge polarity, JKR/SJKR adhesion, capillary forces, or roughness quantitatively. For a charged particle near an ideal conducting wall, the method of images replaces the conductor with an image charge of opposite sign at the same depth below the surface; the particle–image separation is D=2d, and at contact D is approximately 2R. The stated approximation is F_I ≈ −αQ²/(16π epsilon0 R²), with α dependent on particle polarization; α=1.9 is given for dielectric constant κ=4. A 10 μm toner particle with charge-to-mass ratio 15 mC/kg has Q≈8 fC and calculated image adhesion of about 10 nN. Xerography controls cohesion by adding 0.01–1 wt% of 20–40 nm fumed-silica fines, which reduce van der Waals contact area and surface cohesion.

contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant mainly for comparing electrostatic/image-charge adhesion with van der Waals adhesion for micron powders. For a conducting wall, it states that the static image-charge force depends on the square of particle charge. If charge scales linearly with particle size, the estimated image force is approximately size-independent, so it can dominate surface-energy adhesion below a threshold size. If charge instead scales with particle cross-sectional area (approximately size squared), the image force decreases approximately linearly with particle size and surface-energy interactions dominate for sufficiently fine particles. The text does not provide the dielectric-wall image-charge expression involving (epsilon2-epsilon1)/(epsilon2+epsilon1), nor does it specify whether patch charges are opposite or like; it only notes that localized charge patches can significantly affect adhesion. It also does not discuss induced-dipole formulas, capillary forces, PLA/PETG/nylon specifically, or provide a quantitative wall-material comparison experiment. For van der Waals adhesion, the force for a spherical particle near a surface varies linearly with particle radius, while realistic pull-off forces are uncertain because of effective surface energy, roughness, and elastic/plastic deformation. Large soft spheres agree closely with JKR theory, whereas small-particle measurements can be substantially below ideal predictions. Rough particles or particles coated with nanoscale fines may have very low effective van der Waals adhesion. The cited Sternovsky experiment measured tribocharging of Mars simulant particles after repeated contact with cobalt, but numerical results are not included here.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a quantitative framework for electrostatic adhesion, primarily for charged particles near conducting walls. For a point charge, the image charge has equal magnitude and opposite sign, producing attraction; for a finite dielectric particle, induced dipoles and higher multipoles must be included. The approximate conductive-wall expression is FI ≈ −βQ²/[4πε0(Dp+s)²], where s is the particle–wall gap and β accounts for dielectric polarization; β is reported as 1.9 for dielectric constant κ = 4. The monopole expression is explicitly described as a lower bound because polarization increases attraction. Triboelectric charging is often nonuniform, so a uniform surface-charge model can substantially underestimate adhesion: toner centrifuge measurements exceeded predictions by factors of 5–50. A patch-charge model gives an electrostatic contribution proportional to −σ²Ac²/(2ε0), with total adhesion additionally containing a non-electrostatic surface-energy term −WAc. Reported charge densities are 0.5–5 mC/m²; σ = 1 mC/m² and Q = 8 fC yield approximately 100 nN, comparable to measured toner adhesion. contexts.context: The excerpt supports the adhesive-contact portion of the comparison, but it does not provide the requested dielectric image-charge expression, patch-charge sign rules, induced-dipole equations, or PLA/PETG/nylon-versus-conductor experiments. For micron powders, JKR theory gives Fc = −3πγR*, with adhesion scaling linearly with effective particle radius and surface energy. Surface roughness and the true contact area can substantially reduce measured forces relative to ideal smooth-sphere predictions. Typical low-humidity pull-off forces are reported as 2–40 nN for micron-scale particles and tens of nN to approximately 500 nN for 100 μm particles; irregular toner particles around 10 μm showed adhesion as high as 50 nN, nearly two orders of magnitude below smooth-sphere estimates. Plastic deformation becomes possible for sufficiently small particles even without external load because cohesive force decreases more slowly with size than the elastic yielding load. The tabulated threshold diameter for cohesion-driven plastic deformation ranges from 400 μm to 40 mm at E = 1 GPa, 40 μm to 4 mm at 10 GPa, and 4 μm to 400 μm at 100 GPa as surface energy increases from 20 to 2000 mJ/m². The excerpt mentions image-charge forces near conducting surfaces but is truncated before quantitative treatment, and it does not discuss dielectric walls, capillary forces, or SJKR.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not specify a complete recommended Faraday-cup or Faraday-pail Q/m protocol, nor does it provide the requested numerical PA/PC vibrating-wall examples or independent particle-charge validation. It does identify several experimental controls relevant to obtaining reliable powder charge-to-mass measurements. Aggregation and adhesion to the injector tube wall reduce the total measured charge, with cohesion/adhesion becoming particularly important below 1 µm; therefore collected mass and adhered fines should be monitored and reported. Charge aggregates may be as large as millimetres and show a wide surface-charge range, emphasizing the need to characterize the collected population and possible charge heterogeneity. Humidity must be controlled because silica exhibited nearly tenfold higher surface charge concentration around 50% RH, whereas most experiments were conducted below 2% RH. Gas composition also affects charge, with approximately 50% higher charge between argon and CO2, while gas breakdown voltage did not determine charge linearly. Discharges can produce voltage spikes or glow and reduce total charge by up to 6%, so grounding, wall-current monitoring, and discharge rejection are important. Charge reaches a maximum after roughly 38% of injector length, and pressure below 100 mbar reduces cloud charge, making transit history and flow regime necessary controls. Repeated measurements and explicit comparison of cloud charge with independently measured individual-particle charges would address cancellation and collection biases, although these procedures are not detailed here.

A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based models and simulations describe triboelectric charging of powders during feeding, conveying and dosing (condenser model, work-function or surface-state models, DEM with charge transfer plus Coulomb and image forces, CFD-DEM with electrostatics), particularly contacts between metal or salt particles and polymer walls (PLA, PETG, nylon); the effect of humidity and of inert gases (argon, nitrogen) on charge relaxation and gas breakdown; and adhesion of charged fine particles to walls? Which open-source codes implement this, which parameters are needed, and how were the simulations validated (Faraday-cup charge-to-mass ratio)?

# Triboelectric modeling for a 3D-printed auger doser

**Recommendation.** Retain the validated mechanical LIGGGHTS auger model, but treat electrical charging as a separate, experimentally calibrated mechanism. A simulation that predicts salt mass per revolution without fitted parameters has not thereby established the charge transferred at salt–PLA/PETG contacts, the charge retained by an insulating wall, or electrostatic adhesion. Begin with measured outlet charge-to-mass ratio and wall deposition under controlled atmosphere; add charging and electrical forces only where those measurements show that they matter. Published particle–polymer charging models require contact-pair-specific parameters, and humidity can affect charge generation and decay in opposite directions. (pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 31-35, mirkowska2016principalfactorsof pages 9-11, phillips2021implementationofcharged pages 1-4, peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7)

## Physics and required parameters

For repeated particle–wall contacts, a useful *condenser* model is `Δq = k_s A_c(ΔV − k_0q)`: transferred charge depends on maximum contact area, an effective contact-potential difference and the opposing potential created by charge already on the particle. Repetition produces an approximately exponential approach to saturation. Hertzian contact mechanics supplies a first estimate of `A_c`, but its dependence on impact speed, stiffness and real surface roughness matters. Pei’s implementation matched published repeated-impact measurements using this approach; its example `k_s = 10⁻⁴ C m⁻² V⁻¹` is a model parameter, **not** a measured universal constant for the present powders or printed walls. (pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 31-35, pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 102-107, pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 87-92)

For conducting metal–metal contacts, a contact-potential/work-function and capacitance description is a reasonable starting point. An oxidized AlSi10Mg or Al 4047 particle against printed PLA or PETG is instead a metal/oxide–insulator contact: the exposed oxide, adsorbates and polymer surface can govern transfer. Salt, silicon and the organic powders likewise cannot be assigned a reliable charge sign merely from a generic triboelectric series. For two insulating surfaces, occupied and empty surface-state models, mobile-ion transfer and effective contact potentials are alternatives; use measured *effective pair parameters*, rather than assuming that a tabulated metal work function specifies a PLA-, PETG- or nylon-wall collision. Contact charging and electrical conduction during contact should also be distinguished. (pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 35-40, phillips2021implementationofcharged pages 4-7, mirkowska2016principalfactorsof pages 9-11, alchikhsulaiman2020powderspreadingand pages 177-178)

Between contacts, evolve particle charge with an experimentally determined relaxation law, for example `dq/dt = −q/τ_q`; retain charge on insulating wall patches rather than automatically resetting the wall to zero. In contrast, an intentionally grounded conducting insert has a conducting electrical boundary condition, although it still attracts an already charged particle through polarization. Add pairwise Coulomb forces and wall-field forces to the existing Hertz–Mindlin/SJKR/rolling-resistance mechanics; do **not** fold electrostatic adhesion into an increased SJKR surface energy and then count it again as an electric force. For larger particle populations, map charges onto a mesh, solve a Poisson electrostatic problem with appropriate wall boundary conditions, and apply `F = qE`; direct all-pairs summation scales poorly, while a short force cutoff may discard consequential long-range fields. (pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 74-77, goniva2015opensourcecfddem pages 2-3, pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 113-118, walton2008reviewofadhesion pages 1-2)

**Adhesion at the approximately 3 mm outlet.** Compare the local electrostatic force with particle weight and the *separately calibrated* short-range adhesive force. For a charged particle of charge `Q` near an ideal grounded conductor, the simple image-force estimate at contact scales as `Q²/R²`; particle polarization and, especially, charge concentrated on a small contact patch can increase attraction. In one toner comparison, a 10 µm particle carrying about 8 fC gave an approximately 10 nN uniform-charge image-force estimate, yet measured adhesion exceeded such estimates by factors of 5–50. A printed dielectric wall is **not** an ideal grounded image plane: its permittivity contrast, trapped surface charge, conductivity and grounding arrangement determine the field. Roughness can greatly reduce ideal van der Waals pull-off, whereas moisture bridges can increase adhesion even while moisture accelerates electrical leakage. Thus a stopped-auger afterflow or no-flow increment alone cannot identify electrostatic versus capillary or mechanical sticking. (walton2008reviewofadhesion pages 1-2, walton2007adhesionoflunara pages 14-16, walton2008reviewofadhesion pages 5-7)

## Humidity and argon/nitrogen

Model relative humidity and water content as controlled inputs to **both** charge-transfer and charge-decay parameters, and to capillary cohesion. Thin adsorbed-water layers can facilitate mobile-ion transfer; thicker, more conductive layers can discharge surfaces. The resulting trend is material- and timescale-dependent: dry aerosol experiments found that silica surface charge increased almost tenfold near 50% RH, whereas a separate volcanic-ash study found that small amounts of water reduced collected charge by up to an order of magnitude during low-frequency, minute-scale collisions. Neither result supplies a transferable PLA/PETG or salt correction. Record equilibration time, RH, temperature and loss on drying for each powder/wall experiment. (mirkowska2016principalfactorsof pages 9-11, peltonen2019electrostaticinstrumentationand pages 35-38, alois2019contactelectrificationin pages 134-137)

**An inert atmosphere is not an antistatic treatment.** Dry argon and nitrogen still permit contact charging; changing gas also changes adsorbates, gas transport and discharge behavior. In a powder-jet experiment, both Ar and N₂ produced increasing Faraday-cage charge, although visible discharges were less frequent in N₂. Aerosol tests with air, Ar and CO₂ found gas-dependent charging that did not track breakdown voltage linearly. Gas breakdown is a *separate* limit: Paschen/Townsend descriptions depend on gas, pressure, gap and electrode properties. Measurements on 10–500 µm planar gaps found the qualitative breakdown-voltage ordering N₂ above Ar above He, but that geometry cannot provide a numerical breakdown threshold for this doser’s 3 mm outlet or nanometre contact gaps; small gaps and rough surfaces require particular caution. Specify the gas composition, pressure, water content and electrical boundaries rather than assuming that Ar or N₂ neutralizes charge. Likewise, do not invoke plasma Debye screening for an ordinary non-ionized inert atmosphere without evidence of an ionized gas. (alois2019contactelectrificationin pages 134-137, springsklee2023experimentalvolcaniclightning pages 63-67, carazzetti2009electricalbreakdownat pages 3-4, carazzetti2009electricalbreakdownat pages 2-3)

## Open-source implementation and validation status

* **LIGGGHTS-PUBLIC:** the closest documented starting point for the existing auger simulation. Phillips and colleagues modified this open-source DEM code to add contact conduction, work-function/contact-area tribocharging and pairwise standard or screened Coulomb forces, adapting Coulomb source code from **LAMMPS**. Their initial two-particle tests checked charge-transfer and force trends; they were not a Faraday-cup validation for an auger. These features were research modifications, not established default features of a general LIGGGHTS installation. The retrieved papers do not establish a downloadable, version-compatible release of those modifications. (phillips2021implementationofcharged pages 4-7, phillips2021implementationofcharged pages 7-9, phillips2021implementationofcharged pages 1-4)
* **Modified LIGGGHTS with stronger experimental validation:** Wang and colleagues used contact-point electric fields evaluated each timestep, particle–particle and particle–grounded-wall transfer, and electrostatic forces. They compared simulated PA/PC charge-versus-time with both earlier simulations and **Faraday-cage measurements** after 90 s in a grounded, vibrating aluminium box; agreement improved toward the end of the run. Their Figure 3 shows that comparison. The demonstration used millimetre-scale polymer particles, specified charge caps and adjusted contact/shape parameters—not Al alloy or salt fines against printed polymer, and not a parameter-free validation for this feeder. (wang2022investigatingparticleparticleelectrostatic pages 5-7, wang2022investigatingparticleparticleelectrostatic pages 7-8, wang2022investigatingparticleparticleelectrostatic media f4e11fdb)
* **CFDEMcoupling with LIGGGHTS and OpenFOAM:** an open-source framework for particle trajectories and gas momentum/drag exchange. Its documented coupling workflow does **not**, by itself, establish a packaged, validated contact-charging, Poisson-field or polymer-wall image-force solver. Pei’s published condenser-model **DEM–CFD** results and Coulomb/image-force analysis demonstrate modeling methods, but the retrieved account identifies a separately developed DEM–CFD code, not a ready-to-enable CFDEMcoupling module. Add CFD coupling when gas drag, fines entrainment or outlet flight affects the observation; for quasi-static auger contacts, charge-enabled DEM is the less costly first test. (pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 107-113, pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 87-92, goniva2015opensourcecfddem pages 2-3, goniva2015opensourcecfddem pages 1-2)

## Measurement and calibration program

1. **Measure electrical outputs independently of dose mass.** Collect a defined discharged mass in an electrically insulated inner Faraday pail shielded by a grounded outer enclosure; report signed `Q/m` and mass, with a consistent delay after exit. Compare initial and dispensed charge, then recover and weigh powder adhering to the outlet and wall. Vary wall coupons or liners—actual printed PLA, PETG and nylon surfaces versus a specified grounded metal—while controlling gas, RH, powder conditioning, reservoir fill, auger speed, tilt and tap history. Take replicates and measure charge decay after stopping. A pail measures *net* charge: positive and negative grains can cancel, so size-fractionated or single-particle charge measurements are valuable when segregation or bipolar charging is suspected. Published powder measurements demonstrate that changing plastic versus metal contact can change `Q/m` substantially and in a powder-dependent direction. (vyas2021amethodologyto pages 16-24, peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7, peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 4-5, beleca2012investigationofbipolar pages 93-96)
2. **Fit mechanical parameters first, with electrical parameters conditional on those fits.** Use B214/B822 size distributions, particle morphology, B212/B527 packing, D7891/D6773 shear and wall-sensitive measurements, B213/B964 flow, angle of repose and loss on drying as distinct checks on size, packing, friction, cohesion and water sensitivity. Fit the dosing fingerprint—including no-flow frequency, tap-released mass and afterflow—across speeds, tilts and fills. Then use measured `Q/m`, charge decay, wall deposition and charge-versus-contact history to infer separate, pair-specific charging, wall-retention and leakage parameters. Bayesian simulation-based inference should include measurement noise, run-to-run variability and an explicit model-discrepancy term: several combinations of cohesion, wall friction and charge can otherwise explain the same dose. This is a proposed workflow, not an assertion that the cited charging studies recovered unique microscopic properties from auger mass data. (pei2014demcfdanalysisof pages 31-35, mirkowska2016principalfactorsof pages 9-11, vyas2021amethodologyto pages 16-24, peart2001powderelectrostaticstheory pages 5-7)
3. **Control computation and test transferability.** At 26–30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution, reserve full auger evaluations for an informative design of experiments and posterior checks; use cheaper isolated collision/wall-deposition cases and a surrogate for repeated inference. Keep the salt 105 mg/revolution result as a *mechanical baseline*, then compare charge-enabled and charge-disabled predictions on withheld humidity/wall/gas conditions. Finally simulate a representative blade or roller spreading test with the inferred powder parameters and independently measure layer coverage, height variation, density/packing, roughness, streaks and segregation. This last test is essential: a published Bayesian-optimized DEM fit reproduced consolidation void ratio yet produced an excessively cohesive, nonuniform spread layer because consolidation and recoating probe different mechanics. A dosing fingerprint can prioritize powders for AM testing, but cannot on its own certify spreadability. (katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 1-2, katagiri2025bayesianoptimizationbasedparameter pages 11-14, lee2019quantificationofpowder pages 10-14, alchikhsulaiman2020powderspreadingand pages 66-70)

info.query: Context: we run an open-source, 3D-printed (PLA/PETG) auger powder doser for self-driving labs in alloy discovery for additive manufacturing. A small helical auger (1 mL and 10 mL reservoirs, about 3 mm outlet) is turned by a stepper motor at 1-30 rpm, the doser can be tilted 0-30 degrees from horizontal, and a solenoid taps the housing; doses of 0.05-8 g fall onto an analytical balance under closed-loop control. We have dosed 13 powders (NaCl table salt, gas-atomized AlSi10Mg and Al 4047, two silicon grades, rice flour, xanthan gum, carboxymethyl cellulose, BaCl2 and others) and record a 'dosing fingerprint': mass per auger revolution versus tilt and speed, the mass freed by one tap, the afterflow time constant after the auger stops, and the fraction of increments with no flow. A LIGGGHTS DEM model of the auger outlet (Hertz-Mindlin, SJKR cohesion, constant-directional-torque rolling friction) reproduces the measured 105 mg/rev for salt with no fitted parameters but costs 26-30 CPU-minutes per simulated revolution. We want to (i) infer powder properties (cohesion, friction, moisture sensitivity, packing) from dosing data by simulation-based Bayesian calibration, (ii) check the inferred values against standard tests (ASTM D7891 FT4 shear cell, D6773 Schulze ring shear, B213 Hall and B964 Carney flow, B212/B527 apparent and tap density, angle of repose, B214 sieving, B822 laser diffraction, loss on drying), and (iii) anticipate spreadability in powder-bed additive manufacturing. What physics-based models and simulations describe triboelectric charging of powders during feeding, conveying and dosing (condenser model, work-function or surface-state models, DEM with charge transfer plus Coulomb and image forces, CFD-DEM with electrostatics), particularly contacts between metal or salt particles and polymer walls (PLA, PETG, nylon); the effect of humidity and of inert gases (argon, nitrogen) on charge relaxation and gas breakdown; and adhesion of charged fine particles to walls? Which open-source codes implement this, which parameters are needed, and how were the simulations validated (Faraday-cup charge-to-mass ratio)?
